story_text.value:
Hi HN! We're releasing an open-source CLI for hillclimbing Agent Experience. That means optimizing your agent-facing surfaces (Skills, CLIs, SDKs, and docs) so that your users' coding agents can easily use your product. Pointing your own agent at the repo is enough to get started. https://github.com/gauge-sh/gauge-cli

We've found that power users generally want to hand a CLI/MCP to their agents and get started from the terminal. They rarely want to log in and use the web UI themselves. We think developer tools must be agent-friendly to remain relevant.

Here are some common findings that Gauge identifies:

- agents get confused with CLI/SDK behavior and start source diving - interactive commands block agents - agents use deprecated/old CLI commands - agents don't use Skills when you'd expect - agents confidently assert limitations that don't exist - inconsistent terminology confuses agents - agents can't figure out how commands fit together into a workflow

Locally, the Gauge CLI uses Docker containers to run agent harnesses (you can bring your own subscriptions). It finds where agents get confused or stuck and tests changes using your pre-release artifacts (Skills/CLI etc). We normalize events from Claude Code, Codex, Pi and OpenCode into standardized transcripts, and store them locally, alongside structured information in SQLite so that your agent can easily analyze the data. This enables automatic hillclimbing toward a great Agent Experience.

We also offer hosted compute that enables more features, built on our custom Gateway (for credential brokering and transparent, per-session response rewriting). Hosted compute enables many more concurrent sessions, easier collaboration with teammates, a GitHub App for PR reviews, sessions with logged-in MCPs/APIs, and most importantly it lets you close your laptop while the sessions actually run.

You don't need a Gauge account to run the full loop end-to-end though. We expect that local execution with the CLI is enough to find and fix several agent experience issues in a typical project.

You'll be able to validate fixes for these issues locally, before publishing new versions (we inject pre-release Skills and code artifacts into the sessions).

We would love your feedback!

story_text.value:
I've made this app a while ago and now updated it with responsive UI and nice widgets.

Why did I make it?

During my travels to the US and Canada, I wanted to see prices in my currency. however, in both countries, prices are shown BEFORE tax. which adds more confusion.

This conversion apps uses location and locale to try and automatically provide estimations closer to what you'll pay based on your location. It's limited (since tax differs between products) but it's good enough to get a better estimation.

It also includes nice overview of tipping customs (I do hope to make this into an open wiki based if enough demand exists), and Tax Free information.

While I do hope to introduce Android release, It's written in SwiftUI and benefits from Apple's frameworks. so it targets iDevices (iPhone, iPads/Apple Silicon and Apple Watch)

story_text.value:
What’s up HN?! I'm Benji, and I’ve been building Frink since ~April this year.

Frink is a desktop-first, open-source (MIT) app for running coding agents in parallel and multi-step workflows that start on their own. It runs on your machine (macOS and Linux) with your own provider login. It currently supports Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Copilot, and OpenCode, but the latter 3 are in preview. No Frink account to use the app.

The biggest USP of Frink is workflows: think n8n for agents. You describe a routine in a sentence, for example: "every weekday at 9am, run the tests; if any fail, have an agent fix them, then wait for my approval before it opens a PR." Then, Frink builds it as a workflow (or simply, Flow): a list of steps you can read and change before it runs. A Flow can start on a schedule, from any webhook, or from an event from a third-party such as Linear, Shortcut, ClickUp, Sentry, PostHog, etc. Steps can be agent turns, shell commands, conditions, approval steps that stop and wait for you, or steps you write yourself in code (or ask the agent to write one). Everything that needs you (an approval, an agent's question, a finished task to review) lands in one Work Queue.

Other stuff:

* Up to four agents side by side, each on its own git worktree if you want. Or, many agents out of direct view.

* Every change shows as a diff; there's a code editor, a terminal, etc.

* Local-first: chats, Flows and tasks live in SQLite on your machine.

* Easier provider parity: currently working on and improving the tooling setup between providers. Once inside Frink, irrespective of what provider you use, the hooks, MCPs, and other tooling work out of the box between providers.

Why I built it: I started building it when there weren’t many other competitors; now the industry is swamped with ADEs and harnesses. However, in my opinion, each still lacks good automation for more fine-tuned scenarios. I doubled down on the flows to help me with my actual day-to-day job as a SWE, and over time it’s helped me automate most of the PRs being shipped across my personal projects, team, etc., to the point that it’s a continuous loop and helps a whole ton.

Notes: Windows isn't supported yet. Flows only run on Claude Code and Codex for now. It's a solo project, so expect sharp edges.

story_text.value:
CsvPath Framework is a Python data firewall that protects downstream systems from bad data getting past the ingress point. Data is much easier to fix when you shift quality control left, remove manual data checking, stop accumulating orphaned ingestion code, and decrease the skills consumed by data pipelines.

The Framework:

- registers inbound data into an immutable, versioned staging area, with a cryptographic identity,

- validates and upgrades it using one or more of five validation languages,

- generates ops and lineage metadata for OpenLineage and OpenTelemetry,

- and publishes results data and metadata to a versioned immutable archive with no-code integrations downstream.

CsvPath Framework refers to these bullets as "data preboarding".

Supports: JSON Schema, ODCS, XSD, XPath, and CsvPath Validation Language (CVL) validation. Ingests: JSON, JSONL, XML, CSV, Excel, Pandas DataFrames, live Python objects. Backends: AWS, Azure, GCP, SFTP, local; also FlightPath Server

Website: https://www.csvpath.org

story_text.value:
dp_intl is intended to be an enhanced version of the Gettext runtime library (also known as libintl), with the following improvements:

* dp_intl does not depend on the locale. In contrast, Gettext requires the use of the setlocale() function from the C standard library, which alters the behavior of other locale-dependent C routines, leading to subtle bugs that only arise in specific locales. For example, a floating-point number serialized by snprintf() with a locale that uses a period as a decimal separator will not be parsed correctly by strtof() with a locale that uses a comma, and vice versa. Another example is tolower() and strcasecmp(), which will break with the Turkish locale, where the lowercase of "I" is "ı" rather than "i".

* dp_intl uses 64-bit integers for plural form routines on all platforms. In contrast, Gettext routines (e.g. ngettext()) use the unsigned long type, making it impossible to write cross-platform code without limiting your numbers to 2³² (4,294,967,295). Otherwise, translations for numbers greater than 2³² will have incorrect plural forms due to unsigned wrap around (modulo 2³²) on systems with a 32-bit unsigned long (e.g., 64-bit Windows).

* Unlike Gettext, dp_intl is not tied to local file system: it reads files through a virtual stream class that can wrap any file-like object, including those from archives and packages (like an APK on Android).

* dp_intl allows any language in source strings. In contrast, the Gettext routines for translating plural form messages (e.g., ngettext()) are limited to English and several other languages with two plural forms: "one" for 1 and "many" for all other numbers, making it impossible to use any other language that doesn't fit this pattern.

title.value: Show HN: dp_intl – Gettext-compatible internationalization library for C++

story_text.value:
I got into homelabbing a year ago and have been deploying OSS and making some of my own to address some pain points in my everyday life.

One particular area I thought I could improve was keeping in touch with people.

Well that first required having a centralized place to see all my contacts. I have some friends on my Google contacts, other relationships on LinkedIn and even some in Facebook.

A secondary need is something that's been blowing up recently with people search. LLMs + Search are surprisingly good at aggregating relevant data and parsing through for relevant information.

And finally a last need is to keep me disciplined and remind me to reach out to people when it's been a while.

And thus I made Contrack! Aggregate your contacts, smart dedupe, and enrich with people search to get a local repo of your contacts with up-to-date info. Track your contacts as well to remind yourself to keep in touch :)

title.value: Show HN: Contrack – Self-hosted contact manager and people search

story_text.value:
On Sunday, I decide to give it a try and asked Claude to come up with a business idea and run it.

I installed it in an Ubuntu VPS, setup some accounts like Stripe, Cloudflare and let it decide on the idea, stack, promotion, etc.

It created this app: https://pagecritic.app/ that let people evaluate their landing page and scores it on 7 different items, evaluating things like clarify, value prop, CTA and so on.

You can try it for free and get a reduced report, or pay for a full report (first few HN users would be able to get full report for free as well).

The idea was interesting, it was able to build it pretty fast and get it up and running.

I had to help with some account setup, but it basically tried in different ways to launch/promote the app, but distribution is definitely a problem for agent run business.

It can do decent job on get it up and running and react to failures, but in my opinion is not really able to promote the business by itself.

I gave it a channel to Telegram, so it can always ask me for things on Telegram and it did ask for money to pay for advertising it in some launch boards. But still it's not able to really drive much traffic.

The nice thing it did was to make the whole journey public, so you can see it's journal: https://pagecritic.app/journal and some live numbers: https://pagecritic.app/stats

For folks who did similar experiment, has anyone been able to get some substantial revenue out of it? Or this only works if you're an influencer with thousands of followers?

story_text.value:
Hi HN, I'm Hallie, founder of Koody. Today, I'm launching Koody for Business: AI-powered accounting, bookkeeping, and tax prep software for sole proprietors and small businesses.

For years, I used accounting software for my business. I went into it to create invoices, categorize and reconcile transactions, and work with my accountant to prepare our books. I often dreaded having to do it. There were so many transactions to get through in a handful of different currencies, and I found the whole process draining.

The software I used (and refuse to name) worked really well. It was capable accounting software, and I'm not trying to suggest otherwise. But for me, accounting had become a bit like going to the dentist. You know it's necessary and useful, but that doesn't stop you from feeling anxious about it or wishing you didn't have to go.

What makes this personal is that I've always been good at accounting. Throughout secondary school, I was the best student in every financial accounting class. I was also the class prefect, so I would regularly collect everyone's homework and take it to the staff room for submission. My accounting teacher used to ask me to put mine on top because she used it as a marking guide.

I then went on to study finance in undergrad and eventually earned an MBA. So accounting isn't an unfamiliar subject to me, yet dealing with my own books made me extremely sad and anxious.

I'm building Koody for Business because I want business owners to see accounting through my original lens: something simple and enjoyable that doesn't require a degree to understand.

Koody automatically categorizes business income and expenses and uses those transactions to produce cash flow insights, profit and loss reports, and records for Schedule C and tax prep.

There are two workspaces: personal and business. The business workspace lets you manage your business finances separately from your personal finances, even when you use the same bank account for both, as many sole proprietors do. You can keep each transaction in the appropriate workspace, so personal spending stays out of your business reports. You can use Koody just for your business, just for your personal finances, or for both.

Give Koody for Business a try at koody.com/business. I'd love to hear what you think.

title.value: Show HN: Koody for Business – AI bookkeeping for people who aren't accountants

story_text.value:
I have noticed that a lot of job posts that do not use any ATS, and in order to apply, they put their emails and ask candidates to apply with “X” in email subject. That seemed to be very counter productive — imagine having 300+ emails with resumes. Where do you manage them? In Excel? Or how many good candidates you never get to.

I researched popular ATS systems and found out that they require yearly / monthly subscriptions. A lot of them do not have a pricing on the website, so you gotta book a call to be quoted some yearly contract price…

So I built Worklicant — lightweight ATS for tech hiring.

Pay per vacancy. Post a job, share the link, easy application form (no registration needed for applicants). Easy in-app scheduling. Vacancy analytics. Custom hiring stages, tags, notes, application questions.

AI extraction of resume summary, companies, experiences so you do not have to open each resume. You can also write a rejection prompt with ideal candidate description. That will be taken into account when AI (Jev) gives score to each applicant.

I have worked on it for around 2 years on and off so most of the code was hand written (but that’s changing rapidly).

Give it a try and let me know what you think!

title.value: Show HN: Worklicant – Lightweight ATS. Pay per Vacancy. AI Enabled

I have noticed that a lot of job posts that do not use any ATS, and in order to apply, they put their emails and ask candidates to apply with “X” in email subject. That seemed to be very counter productive — imagine having 300+ emails with resumes. Where do you manage them? In Excel? Or how many good candidates you never get to.

I researched popular ATS systems and found out that they require yearly / monthly subscriptions. A lot of them do not have a pricing on the website, so you gotta book a call to be quoted some yearly contract price…

So I built Worklicant — lightweight ATS for tech hiring.

Pay per vacancy. Post a job, share the link, easy application form (no registration needed for applicants). Easy in-app scheduling. Vacancy analytics. Custom hiring stages, tags, notes, application questions.

AI extraction of resume summary, companies, experiences so you do not have to open each resume. You can also write a rejection prompt with ideal candidate description. That will be taken into account when AI (Jev) gives score to each applicant.

I have worked on it for around 2 years on and off so most of the code was hand written (but that’s changing rapidly).

Give it a try and let me know what you think!
hits.title: Show HN: Worklicant – Lightweight ATS. Pay per Vacancy. AI Enabled

story_text.value:
I often switch between Claude Code and Codex throughout the week, and between my laptop and an older machine I leave running at home. I built agent-archive to make it easier to pick up where I left off, especially when i hit usage limits.

It lets you (or a coding agent) find past coding sessions and hand their conversation context to another agent. You can try local handoffs without setup, or connect your own S3/R2 bucket for automatic archiving and access from other machines.

It also tracks usage across agents and gives you a full archive of your session transcripts across agents, which I've found useful to iterating and improving my AGENTS.md and lint rules.

story_text.value:
I run long sessions with Claude. For a long time I've had Claude in the middle of some difficult coding task, and then I see the auto-compact message pop up. Every time I wonder if Claude actually picks everything up correctly and nothing is lost. Claude told me 78/82 auto-compactions landed while Claude was working. For a while I couldn't do much. At first I made a skill that would make Claude explicitly save progress throughout long runs. But that didn't fix the core problem and cost more tokens as well. Now that mods came out, I fixed the actual problem.

catnap tells Claude at 50% context what the context is and that it should finish what it's working on, write a handoff, and then initialize compaction itself. When Claude finishes its task, catnap compacts, and Claude can then pick up work again. The handoff replaces Claude Code's default summary, so we don't do similar work twice. If Claude for some reason doesn't compact before 60%, it gets a stricter note. And Claude Code's default auto-compact kicks in at 70% as a backstop. The 3 numbers are all settings.

After I took on catnap, 0 of 129 naps came mid-task: 98 of them in benchmarks and 31 in my own sessions.

The cost is the same as the default auto-compact kicking in at the same point, in tokens and dollars, on 200K and 1M context windows. Compared to the default auto-compaction that kicks in when context is nearly full, catnap used 56% fewer tokens. But lowering the default auto-compact will get you most of the way there as well.

I measured memory today as well. Claude worked through tasks one message at a time while 20 instructions and facts were said in the chat, inside long chatty messages, and nowhere else. Asked right after compaction to list them from memory, no file reads: all 20 were listed with catnap and with the default compaction, in every run (15 with catnap, 5 with the default). So in my tests the memory was exactly the same, but catnap got there with a handoff 60% shorter (4.0K tokens against 10K).

I was surprised that catnap is actually faster than the default option. This wasn't even one of the reasons I wanted to make this, it just happened. Since Claude writes the handoff in one go instead of the separate summary call the default makes, and the note is shorter, tasks finish sooner: measured end to end, 406 seconds instead of 464.

Try it with nothing installed:

  npx github:LippInc/catnap
It prints how often auto-compact cut in mid-task in your own logs (reads numbers only, sends nothing).

Install (needs Claude Code 2.1.287 or later, where mods are on by default):

  claude plugin marketplace add LippInc/catnap
  claude plugin install catnap@lippinc
Currently Claude Code only, tested on Windows and Linux. The memory test used made-up coding tasks on a 200K window.

Some related tools: compact-adviser, handoff-compact, session-pilot and sub-agent-compact. What catnap adds: Claude finishes its piece first, and the numbers on where the cut lands.
